To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) Dory is an efficient, transparent setup, public coin interactive argument for proving the correctness of an inner pairing product between two committed vectors of elements from two source groups; 2) Dory can be used to construct an efficient, transparent, polynomial commitment scheme that can be used to prove the correctness of a polynomial evaluation.

we present Dory, a public-coin, transparent, interactive argument of knowledge for proving correctness of the inner pairing product between two committed vectors of elements from the two source groups of an asymmetric bilinear map, with proofs that are 6log n target group elements (where n is the size of the two vectors), and that we show how to use it to build a multilinear polynomial commitment scheme with a similar communication complexity and Verifiers work complexity, but with much lower Prover work complexity.

Dory is a transparent setup, interactive argument for proving the correctness of an inner product between committed vectors, and a polynomial commitment scheme, both of which can be used to construct a succinct argument system.

we have presented a new interactive protocol for proving correctness of a pairing product, which is secure under the SDH assumption, has a very low communication cost and low verifier computation cost.

we have a new transparent argument system for inner products that is secure in the standard model under a natural assumption and that can be applied to polynomial commitment schemes with a number of attractive features.

Dory is a new, efficient and transparent argument system for proving inner product relations between committed vectors, which is the first to provide a formal security analysis in the standard model, and which can be used to efficiently construct a new multivariate polynomial commitment with similar efficiency to the state-of-the-art.

we can build a general purpose, transparent polynomial commitment scheme that is as fast and efficient as existing schemes for specific classes of polynomials, whilst being more general.
